slides.speaker_notes:
[0:00 - 0:15 | Slide 1: Introduction]
Judges, this is ReturnLens. For independent online sellers, returns are exhausting. When a customer claims they received the wrong product, the solo merchant is stuck cross-referencing customer chat, Shopify orders, and courier tracking just to figure out what happened. ReturnLens unifies customer claims, video evidence, and store rules into one simple decision pack. Notice our core button: 'Review Evidence & Decide'. We never automate refunds or rejections. The model observes, our code verifies, but the seller always authorizes the decision.

slides.decision_dilemma: THE CORE DILEMMA: Is this a warehouse packing error, an honest customer mix-up, or an unboxing swap? Automatic refunds destroy profit margins; automatic rejections destroy customer trust. The merchant needs verified facts to choose the next step.
slides.speaker_notes:
[0:15 - 0:40 | Slide 2: The Problem]
A customer chats in: 'You sent the wrong color, refund me immediately' and attaches an unboxing clip. Right now, the merchant has to jump across four separate tabs: checking the chat claim, looking up the SKU in Shopify, verifying courier delivery on Shippo, and re-reading their store return policy. Was this a warehouse mix-up, an honest confusion, or an item swap? Blindly refunding burns scarce margin, but blindly rejecting the customer destroys brand loyalty. Solo merchants don't have a fraud department—they need a unified view of the facts.

slides.prepared_pack_title: WHAT RETURNLENS PREPARES FOR THE MERCHANT:

options.title: Accept warehouse mis-pack
options.desc: Warehouse staff likely grabbed black inventory by mistake. Issue replacement return label.

options.title: Request box label photo
options.desc: Ask customer for a quick photo of the barcode on the outer shipping box to trace parcel origin.

options.title: Hold for inspection
options.desc: Approve physical return, but hold refund release until parcel is inspected at warehouse.

slides.disclaimer: * Illustrative concept scenario with staged mock evidence. Not live production video footage.
slides.speaker_notes:
[0:40 - 1:25 | Slide 3: The Core Demonstration]
Here is our core demonstration. The Shopify order clearly specifies Matte White headphones. But in the unboxing clip at frame seven seconds, the customer unboxes black headphones. ReturnLens instantly flags this visible color mismatch. Crucially, we practice honest AI grounding: our agent acknowledges that the barcode and exact SKU are unverified from the video frame. We do not jump to calling the customer a fraudster—this could easily be a warehouse packing error. Instead, ReturnLens presents three clear, practical options with drafted customer replies ready for the seller to approve.

slides.title: Models observe. Code verifies. Seller authorizes.
slides.subtitle: A structured agent pipeline that investigates, checks policies, and drafts the next step.

pipeline_steps.desc: Ingests customer chat, order records, carrier tracking, and extracts cited keyframes.
Cross-checks observed visual traits against catalog truth, delivery date, and 7-day policy.
Synthesizes matches, conflicts, or missing evidence into 3 actionable resolution paths.
Seller reviews the evidence pack and clicks one button to confirm the action.

clarification_loop.title: DYNAMIC CLARIFICATION (CASE C):
clarification_loop.desc: If video is dark or blurry (<50/255 luminance), agent asks customer for 1 guided re-upload, pauses case in WAITING_FOR_EVIDENCE, and automatically resumes when new footage arrives. Max 1 retry before escalating to seller.

roles_breakdown.detail: Vision and language models transcribe claims, cite keyframe timestamps, and draft replies.
Deterministic Python code calculates return windows, delivery validity, and refund limits.
Human seller retains full authority. Zero automated refunds; zero automated customer denials.

slides.speaker_notes:
[1:25 - 2:05 | Slide 4: How the Agent Moves the Case Forward]
How does the agent actually work? It follows four clear stages: First, Collect—ingesting the chat, tracking data, and video keyframes. Second, Compare—deterministic code verifies the 7-day window and checks color alignment. Third, Recommend—the agent drafts clear resolution choices. And fourth, Authorize—the merchant makes the call. If evidence is dark or blurry, like in our Case C, the agent guides the customer to turn on a light, pauses the case, and resumes when the new clip arrives. Notice the clean separation: models observe, code verifies rules, and the human seller authorizes.

slides.title: Three situations. Three useful next steps.
slides.subtitle: ReturnLens handles clean claims, flags discrepancies, and guides unclear evidence.

columns.title: Consistent Claim
columns.situation: Unboxing footage clearly shows cracked headphone headband upon box opening. Within 4-day delivery window.
columns.agent_action: Validates delivery date and visible physical damage; drafts return shipping label for merchant review.
columns.seller_outcome: 1-click approval to issue return label. Refund remains pending until parcel is scanned at warehouse.

columns.title: Color Discrepancy
columns.situation: Customer claims defective white headphones, but unboxing video shows black casing.
columns.agent_action: Halts auto-routing; highlights color mismatch; notes barcode is unverified; prepares 3 resolution options.
columns.seller_outcome: Seller decides: accept warehouse packing error, ask for outer box photo, or hold return for inspection.

columns.title: Unclear Evidence
columns.situation: 4-second dark, shaky unboxing video (<50/255 brightness score). Product condition cannot be verified.
columns.agent_action: Guides customer with tips to re-film in good light; pauses case; resumes seamlessly on new upload.
columns.seller_outcome: Customer gets a fair chance to clarify. If 2nd attempt fails, escalates directly to seller with full history.

slides.footer_note: * Expected prototype behavior across core test scenarios. Advanced video forensics (Case D) reserved as stretch goal.
slides.speaker_notes:
[2:05 - 2:30 | Slide 5: Three Scenarios]
In our prototype, we focus on three core situations that represent 95% of returns: In Case A, the evidence is consistent—a visible crack on arrival. The agent drafts a return label ready for one-click approval. In Case B, there is a color discrepancy—the agent surfaces the conflict and offers options without accusing the customer. In Case C, the footage is too dark—instead of rejecting the customer, the agent politely asks for a clearer clip with helpful tips. Each scenario leads to an actionable, low-stress outcome for the solo merchant.

slides.speaker_notes:
[2:30 - 3:00 | Slide 6: Execution Roadmap & Closing]
For this 24-hour hackathon, our scope is strictly disciplined: Person A builds the state machine and policy checks; Person B builds the keyframe viewer and merchant console; Person C prepares realistic mock fixtures and tests all three scenarios. We are not building live Shopify webhooks or banking integrations during the sprint—our focus is proving the end-to-end evidence triage workflow. ReturnLens gives solo online sellers the clarity of a full-scale returns department, while keeping every decision firmly in human hands. Thank you!

qa_defense.question: Why do you need an agent instead of a simple form or rules engine?
qa_defense.answer: A standard rules engine can only check structured database fields like dates. It cannot inspect unboxing video keyframes, identify product colors, handle customer clarification dialogues, or synthesize contradictory evidence into a coherent decision pack. The agent bridges messy multimodal customer input with strict merchant policies.

qa_defense.question: Why doesn't a color discrepancy prove customer fraud?
qa_defense.answer: A color discrepancy only indicates that the product in the video differs from the Shopify order. It could easily be a warehouse shipping mistake, an order fulfillment mix-up, or the customer opening a family member's parcel by mistake. Accusing the customer of fraud destroys goodwill; presenting choices lets the merchant decide based on their knowledge of their warehouse accuracy.

qa_defense.question: What happens when unboxing video footage is dark, blurry, or inconclusive?
qa_defense.answer: In our Case C flow, ReturnLens activates Policy P-06. Rather than auto-rejecting the customer, the agent sends helpful guidance (e.g. 'Please film under good lighting so we can see the product serial number and seal'), pauses the ticket, and resumes when the customer uploads new footage. If the second attempt fails, it escalates to the merchant with the full video history.

qa_defense.question: What authority does the merchant retain in this system?
qa_defense.answer: The merchant retains 100% decision authority. ReturnLens is strictly fail-closed: it has zero authority to issue payments, trigger chargebacks, or send rejection notices on its own. It prepares drafted return options and drafted messages, but every consequential action requires a one-click merchant confirmation.

qa_defense.question: What does your 24-hour prototype actually prove?
qa_defense.answer: Our 24-hour prototype proves the end-to-end feasibility of multimodal return triage: extracting keyframes, running deterministic rule checks, handling a dynamic clarification loop, and generating an actionable decision console for the seller across three realistic benchmark scenarios.
